855.title: A threefold cord (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
855.hook: two are better than one, and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken"
855.carry: woe to him that is alone
855.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is studied in Jewish teaching on friendship and community, and some readers take the third strand as God between two people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's poem of pairs: to every thing there is a season. Your line was a time for everything. Today, Kohelet stops looking at time and looks at the people beside us.

Pull a single thread from the hem of a shirt and snap it between your fingers. Easy. Now take three threads, twist them together, and try again. It bites into your skin. It holds. The strength isn't in one heroic strand. It's in ordinary strands wound around each other. Kohelet, the man who called everything breath, noticed the same thing about people.
screen: `ONE THREAD SNAPS.` → `THREE THREADS, TWISTED, HOLD.` → `NOT BEING ALONE.`

segments.voice: Just before this passage, Kohelet describes a man entirely alone. No child, no brother, and yet no end to his work, and his eyes never satisfied with riches. He never stops to ask who he's laboring for. That is hevel, Kohelet says. Breath. Then he turns, in the King James words: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Three small pictures follow. The first: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." A stumble on a road, and a hand reaching down. The second: if two lie together, they have heat, but how can one be warm alone? The third: if one is attacked, two can stand against the attacker. Then the line that stays: "a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Wait. He's been talking about two. Where does the third strand come from? Some say it simply means: if two are strong, three are stronger still. Some see the third strand as God, woven between two people. Others see a community, the circle that holds a pair together. The text leaves it unnamed. And notice the word quickly. Not never broken. A cord can still fray. But wound together, it takes longer, and that gives time for someone to come and help.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you care about but haven't really talked to in a while, and picture where they might be right now and what their day looks like. Think of one small thread you could add, a message, a question about something they care about, a memory you share. If you pray, you can pray for that friend by name; if not, hold their name gently for a while.

856.title: Eat thy bread with joy (Ecclesiastes 9:7–10)
856.hook: enjoy your life, and do what your hand finds to do with all your might
856.howItsDone: Before eating bread, Jews say a blessing, hamotzi, thanking God who brings forth bread from the earth, and after the meal they say a grace, Birkat Hamazon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two are better than one, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Your line was woe to him that is alone. Today, Kohelet, of all people, says enjoy your food.

Lunch, eaten standing up. One hand holds the sandwich, the other scrolls. Somewhere around the fourth bite the sandwich is gone, and there's no memory of how it tasted. The mind was three meetings ahead the whole time. Now listen to who's about to talk about this: Kohelet, the man who said all is breath, who watched the wise die like the foolish. You might expect him to say food doesn't matter either. He says the opposite.
screen: `LUNCH, EATEN STANDING UP.` → `NO MEMORY OF THE TASTE.` → `KOHELET SAYS THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes nine, in the King James words: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works." Go thy way: almost a dismissal. Stop worrying, go and eat. And the reason isn't that you've earned it. God now accepteth thy works. In his telling, the meal isn't a reward to be won later; the acceptance has come first. Then Kohelet piles up ordinary gifts. Let your clothes be white, and your head not lack oil: dress for a good day. Live joyfully with the wife you love, all the days of your fleeting life. The Hebrew for those days is the word from a few days ago, hevel. Breath. That's the turn. Kohelet doesn't say enjoy life because it lasts. He says enjoy it because it doesn't. Breath is short, so taste the bread. Then the verse that gives the joy some muscle: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest." A sobering reason, given straight. The work in front of you is yours now, not later. So this isn't a call to idle pleasure. It's two halves of one way of living: eat with joy, and work with your whole strength. Some readers hear these lines as the quiet heart of the whole book, where its doubt and its gladness meet.

Jewish practice sets a blessing before eating; if you pray, you can say the one you know, and if not, a moment of thanks is enough.

857.title: Cast thy bread (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
857.hook: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days"
857.carry: thou knowest not which shall prosper
857.howItsDone: Some Jewish commentators read Ecclesiastes 11:1 as a teaching about kindness and tzedakah given with no promise of return; in some communities the book of Ecclesiastes is read aloud in synagogue on Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet said eat thy bread with joy, and do it with thy might. Today the same book sends the bread down a river.

Bread, tossed from a riverbank onto moving water. It floats a second, turns, and the current takes it. By any normal reckoning, that bread is gone. Nobody gets a receipt from a river. Yet near the end of Ecclesiastes, the book that kept saying all is breath, comes this odd instruction: "Cast thy bread upon the waters, For thou shalt find it after many days." Let it go, says the teacher, and it will come back to you.
screen: `BREAD ON MOVING WATER.` → `NO RECEIPT FROM A RIVER.` → `IT WILL COME BACK.`

segments.voice: The verse never says how the bread comes back, or when, beyond after many days. So readers fill the gap in different ways. Some hear a merchant's advice: send your goods across the sea, and the profit returns in time. Some hear charity: give to people who can never repay you, and the good finds its way home. The commentator Rashi reads it as kindness done for someone you expect never to see again. The next verse keeps the hand open: "Divide a portion into seven, yea, even into eight; For thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth." Not one gift, carefully placed. Seven shares, and then one more. Then Kohelet turns to the person who waits for perfect conditions: "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; And he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap." Stand in the field checking the sky, and the seed stays in the bag. Then the line that ties it together: "In the morning sow thy seed, And in the evening withhold not thy hand; For thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that." Notice what the teacher doesn't promise. He doesn't say every gift returns. He says you don't know. That not-knowing, which earlier in the book made everything feel like breath, becomes here the reason to keep giving. The bread on the water isn't an investment with a guaranteed return. It's a gift, let go.

858.title: The holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5)
858.hook: Rabbi Akiva called the Song of Songs the holy of holies among the writings
858.tomorrow: I am my beloved's (Song of Songs 6:3)
858.howItsDone: In Ashkenazi custom the Song of Songs is read in synagogue during Passover, and in some communities it is recited on Friday evening before the Sabbath begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet said sow, for thou knowest not which shall prosper. Today, a love song, and a rabbi who called it holy.

Why is a book of love poetry in the Bible at all? Open the Song of Songs and you'll find kisses, a garden, a lover leaping over the hills like a gazelle, a woman searching the city streets at night for the one she loves. No laws. No kings at war. No prophets thundering. The rabbis of the Mishnah asked a version of that question out loud, and one of them answered with startling praise.
screen: `A BOOK OF LOVE POETRY.` → `NO LAWS, NO KINGS AT WAR.` → `WHY IS IT HERE?`

segments.voice: Shir HaShirim, the Song of Songs. Hebrew can say the best of something by doubling a word. The holy of holies is the holiest place; the song of songs, by the same pattern, is a song above songs. The book's first verse names it: "The song of songs, which is Solomon's." In the Mishnah, tractate Yadayim, the rabbis discuss which books are holy scripture. Their way of putting it is unusual: a holy scroll is one that makes the hands impure, so you wash after handling it. Some there said the Song was in dispute. Rabbi Akiva would have none of it. In the Mishnah's telling he says, in effect: heaven forbid. No one in Israel ever doubted the Song. The whole world was not as worthy as the day it was given to Israel. All the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. Why say that about a love poem? Rabbinic midrash, such as Song of Songs Rabbah, reads it as the love between God and the people of Israel: the lover is God, the beloved is the people, and the searching and finding are their story together. Other readers hear it first as human love, and see no need to choose. Akiva's phrase can hold both: a song so close to the heart it belongs in the innermost room. The Song even keeps a calendar. "For, lo, the winter is past, The rain is over and gone," it says in its second chapter, and it's read in synagogue in the spring, at Passover. Holy of holies, and also love letters.

segments.voice: If a Bible is nearby, open the Song of Songs anywhere and read one verse slowly, twice; if not, take the line from chapter two: the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Ask what kind of love it might describe, between two people, between God and a people, or both, and leave the question open. If you pray, read it as slowly as you would a prayer.

859.title: I am my beloved's (Song of Songs 6:3)
859.hook: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine"; tradition hears the month of Elul in its first letters
859.howItsDone: The verse 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine' is taught as a hint to the name of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, when Ashkenazi communities sound the shofar on weekday mornings and add Psalm 27 to the prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shir HaShirim: Rabbi Akiva called a love poem the holy of holies, a song above songs. Today, one line from inside that poem.

Four Hebrew letters: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. Together they spell Elul, the month just before Rosh Hashanah. Tradition says that month is hiding inside one line of the Song of Songs. Take the first letter of each of the line's first four Hebrew words, set them side by side, and there it is. A love song, carrying the name of a month on the calendar.
screen: `ALEPH, LAMED, VAV, LAMED.` → `ELUL, THE MONTH BEFORE ROSH HASHANAH.` → `HIDDEN IN ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: I am my beloved's. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, That feedeth among the lilies." In Hebrew: ani l'dodi v'dodi li. Ani, I. L'dodi, to my beloved. V'dodi, and my beloved. Li, to me. Aleph, lamed, vav, lamed: Elul. Earlier in the Song, nearly the same words come in the other order: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Some readers notice the turn. First she says he is hers. Later she begins with herself, given to him. Love that starts with having becomes love that starts with giving. Why tie the line to Elul? Elul is the month of getting ready for the High Holy Days. In Ashkenazi custom the shofar is sounded on weekday mornings through the month, until the day before Rosh Hashanah, and Psalm twenty-seven is added to the daily prayers. It's a month for looking back, setting things right with people, and turning. The teaching about the letters, from later Jewish writers, says this turning needn't be a grim inspection. It can be two who love each other walking back toward each other. Read that way, the people say the first half to God, I am my beloved's, and God's answer is folded into the same sentence: and my beloved is mine. The line has another life too. Some couples engrave it inside wedding rings or speak it under the wedding canopy. The same four words carry a marriage and a month of return.

860.title: Strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6–7)
860.hook: "love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench love"
860.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the Song of Songs as love between God and Israel as well as between people, and some couples use the words 'set me as a seal upon thy heart' at their weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dodi, my beloved, in the line whose first letters spell Elul. Your line was love that starts with giving. Today, near its last page, the Song makes a bold claim about love.

"Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it." Floods are an old picture of a force nothing stops. In Genesis the waters rise until the mountains are covered. Here, near the end of the Song of Songs, the waters meet something they can't put out. The woman in the Song asks her beloved to keep her close, and then tells him why: love holds on as hard as the one thing nobody escapes.
screen: `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` → `A FIRE THE FLOODS CAN'T PUT OUT.` → `AS STRONG AS WHAT NOBODY ESCAPES.`

segments.voice: Strong as death. The verse just before, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD." A seal is a mark that says whose something is. Set me as a seal: wear me where you can't forget me, on your heart and on your arm. In Hebrew the line runs azzah khamavet ahavah: strong as death, love. Death doesn't give back what it takes. The Song says love holds on just as hard. Not gentler than death. Equal to it. Then the flame. The verse's last Hebrew word is shalhevetyah, and its last syllable, yah, is also a short form of God's name. The JPS translators heard it that way: a very flame of the LORD. Others take the yah as a way of saying a mighty flame. The text lets it flicker both ways. Then the floods. Water puts out fire; that's what water does. Except this fire. And the verse closes with a warning: "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned." Love can't be bought. It can only be kept burning. And notice what the Song doesn't claim. It doesn't call love gentle, or easy, or safe; in the same breath it says jealousy is cruel as the grave. It calls love strong.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL UPON THY HEART.` · `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.` · then, large: `A FLAME CALLED SHALHEVETYAH.` · then: `LOVE CAN'T BE BOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a love that has been tested, by distance, by time, by a hard season, maybe by a death; it might be someone still here, or someone you still love who is gone. Rest a hand on your heart, where the Song asks to be worn like a seal, and hold that person there for a few slow breaths, asking nothing of the memory. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers.
Azzah. Hebrew for strong: the Song's claim that love holds on as hard as death does, and many waters cannot quench it. Today's word.
Your line: many waters cannot quench it. No flood puts this fire out. See you tomorrow.

861.title: How doth the city sit (Lamentations 1:1)
861.hook: the city once full of people sits solitary, like a widow
861.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, the fast for the destruction of the Temples, Lamentations is chanted in synagogue in a mournful melody while people sit on the floor or on low stools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, azzah: the Song said love is strong as death, and many waters cannot quench it. This week ran from a threefold cord, to bread cast on the water, to the Song's holy of holies. Today, a different kind of song.

A city, drawn as a woman, sitting on the ground. The streets around her used to be loud with people. Now nobody comes. That's the opening picture of the book of Lamentations, and it begins with one sighing word, eichah, how. Earlier on this path we heard that word chanted on Tisha B'Av, the fast for the Temples. Today we stay with the picture that follows it.
screen: `A CITY, DRAWN AS A WOMAN.` → `THE LOUD STREETS GONE QUIET.` → `ONE SIGHING WORD.`

segments.voice: How doth the city sit. The first verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "How doth the city sit solitary, That was full of people! How is she become as a widow! She that was great among the nations, And princess among the provinces, How is she become tributary!" Three pictures, one after another. Full of people, now alone. A wife, now a widow. A princess, now paying tribute. Each is a fall from a height, and each is about a person, not a pile of stones. Lamentations doesn't describe Jerusalem's ruins like a report. It turns the city into someone you could sit beside. Then it shows her at night: "She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers." Tears on her cheeks. Not falling, just there, the way tears stay when no one has come to wipe them. The chapter keeps coming back to those words: none to comfort her. The book doesn't argue. It doesn't hurry to explain why it happened, or how it will be fixed. It sits. Eichah isn't a question waiting for an answer. It's a cry. And the city's posture becomes the posture of the people who read it: on Tisha B'Av, mourners sit low, on the floor or on low stools, while the book is chanted. Sometimes the honest thing a text can do is refuse to stand up too fast. And now someone is sitting with her: the one reading.
screen: `FULL OF PEOPLE, NOW ALONE.` · `A WIDOW, A PRINCESS PAYING TRIBUTE.` · then, large: `NONE TO COMFORT HER.` · then: `THE READER SITS WITH HER.`

segments.voice: Find a quiet room if you can, or turn away from the screens around you, and sit down. Notice the quiet and what's missing from it, voices, footsteps, someone who used to be there, and don't fill it; if a loss comes to mind, yours or the world's, let it sit beside you. If you pray, let the silence be part of your prayer.
Eichah. The sighing word that opens Lamentations: Jerusalem, once full of people, sitting alone like a widow. Today's word.
Your line: how she sits alone. The book keeps her company before it says anything else. Day eight hundred sixty-one.
